title: Connect tangents and accumulated area
goal: Connect tangents and accumulated area. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: Differential calculus asks for an instantaneous rate; integral calculus adds continuously varying contributions. Limits connect finite approximations to these quantities.
steps: Take s(t)=t² meters and look near t=2 seconds.
The average rate over [2,2+h] is ((2+h)²−4)/h=4+h.
Values for h=0.1 and 0.01 are 4.1 and 4.01 m/s.
The limiting rate is 4 m/s, the tangent slope.

title: Estimate limits without trusting a table alone
goal: Estimate limits without trusting a table alone. Explain your method and its conditions.

title: Check one-sided limits and continuity
goal: Check one-sided limits and continuity. Explain your method and its conditions.

The left limit at 2 is 3.
The right limit and f(2) are also 3.

title: A sequence is a list with a destination
goal: Find a sequence’s limit and explain what convergence actually means.
idea: A sequence aₙ gives one number for each positive integer n. Convergence to L means every term sufficiently far along is as close to L as you demand. It does not mean a term eventually equals L.
steps: Divide numerator and denominator by n: aₙ = (3 + 2/n)/(1 + 1/n).
As n grows, both fractions involving 1/n approach zero, so the limit is 3.
For an accuracy of 0.01, solve |aₙ − 3| = 1/(n + 1) < 0.01. Every n ≥ 100 works.
The terms increase toward 3 from below. This pattern supports the calculation; a graph alone is not a proof.
trap: Oscillation matters. (−1)ⁿ has no limit, although it stays bounded. In contrast, (−1)ⁿ/n converges to 0 because the oscillation shrinks.

solution: No. The even terms approach 2 and the odd terms approach −2. Two subsequences with different limits rule out one common limit.

title: A series is a sequence of running totals
goal: Separate terms aₙ from partial sums Sₙ, and evaluate a geometric series.
idea: A sequence asks where individual terms go. A series asks where their accumulated total goes. We define an infinite sum using the limit of its finite partial sums—not by pretending we can finish adding infinitely many terms.
formula: Sₙ = a₁ + a₂ + ⋯ + aₙ       ∑ aₙ converges exactly when Sₙ has a finite limit.
steps: Consider 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ⋯. Its terms go to zero, but we still need the totals.
After N terms, Sₙ = 1 − 2⁻ᴺ. For example, S₁ = 0.5, S₂ = 0.75 and S₃ = 0.875.
As N → ∞, 2⁻ᴺ → 0, so the infinite sum is 1.
More generally, a + ar + ar² + ⋯ = a/(1 − r) when |r| < 1. If a ≠ 0 and |r| ≥ 1, it diverges.
trap: aₙ → 0 is necessary, not sufficient. The harmonic series ∑1/n diverges even though 1/n → 0. If aₙ does not approach 0, divergence is immediate.
challenge: Evaluate ∑ₙ₌₀∞ 3(−1/2)ⁿ.
solution: The first term is a = 3 and the ratio is r = −1/2. Since |r| < 1, the sum is 3/[1 − (−1/2)] = 2. Partial sums alternate above and below 2.

title: Choose a test by the shape of the terms
goal: Use p-series, comparison and the integral test with the required conditions.
idea: For nonnegative terms, partial sums only grow. Convergence asks whether that growth stays bounded. Compare with a series whose behavior you already understand.
formula: ∑ₙ₌₁∞ 1/nᵖ converges if p > 1; diverges if p ≤ 1.
steps: The benchmark ∑1/n² converges because p = 2 > 1.
A smaller nonnegative series also converges, by direct comparison.
For ∑ n/(n² + 1), compare with 1/n instead. The ratio [n/(n² + 1)]/(1/n) approaches 1, a positive finite number. Limit comparison shows both diverge.
trap: A convergent smaller series says nothing about a larger one. Use: smaller than a convergent upper bound ⇒ convergence; larger than a divergent lower bound ⇒ divergence.
challenge: Determine whether ∑ₙ₌₂∞ 1/[n(ln n)²] converges.
solution: f(x) = 1/[x(ln x)²] is positive, continuous and decreasing for x ≥ 2. Substitution u = ln x gives ∫₂∞ f(x) dx = 1/ln 2, which is finite. The integral test proves convergence; it does not say the sum equals the integral.

questions.prompt: Does ∑ₙ₌₁∞ 1/n⁰·⁸ converge?

questions.hint: It is a p-series with p = 0.8.
questions.explain: The series diverges. Terms approaching zero do not guarantee a finite total.

title: Alternating sums: convergence and honest accuracy
goal: Distinguish absolute from conditional convergence and bound truncation error.
idea: Alternating signs can produce cancellation. If positive magnitudes bₙ eventually decrease to zero, the alternating series converges. Check absolute convergence separately by removing the signs.
formula: For an alternating series with decreasing bₙ → 0:   |S − Sₙ| ≤ bₙ₊₁.
steps: The alternating harmonic series 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − ⋯ converges: bₙ = 1/n decreases to zero.
The absolute-value series ∑1/n diverges. Therefore the original series is conditionally convergent.
After N terms, the absolute error is at most 1/(N + 1).
To guarantee error < 0.01, choose N = 100: 1/101 < 0.01. With N = 99 the bound is only ≤ 0.01, not strictly less.
trap: Alternating signs alone do not prove convergence. ∑(−1)ⁿ diverges because the terms do not approach zero. The next-term error bound also requires the alternating/decreasing conditions.
challenge: Classify ∑ₙ₌₁∞ (−1)ⁿ⁻¹/n² and bound the error after 10 terms.
solution: It converges absolutely because ∑1/n² converges. It is also alternating with decreasing magnitudes, so its 10-term truncation error is at most 1/11² = 1/121 ≈ 0.008264.

title: Factorials and exponentials: ratio or root?
goal: Apply ratio/root tests without overinterpreting a limit of 1.
idea: The ratio test asks how each term compares with the previous one. The root test asks for its effective exponential factor. Both detect tails that shrink at least geometrically.
formula: L = lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ|  or  lim ⁿ√|aₙ|:   L < 1 ⇒ absolute convergence; L > 1 ⇒ divergence; L = 1 ⇒ inconclusive.
steps: For ∑ₙ₌₁∞ n/3ⁿ, compute |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = [(n + 1)/n] · 1/3.
The limit is 1/3, which is below 1. The series converges absolutely.
For ∑ₙ₌₁∞ n!/4ⁿ, the ratio is (n + 1)/4, which tends to infinity. The series diverges.
For ∑(n/(2n + 1))ⁿ, the nth root of the term tends to 1/2. The root test proves convergence.
trap: L = 1 means choose another test. Both ∑1/n and ∑1/n² have ratio-test limit 1, but only the second converges.
challenge: Classify ∑ₙ₌₀∞ 2ⁿ/n!.
solution: The ratio of consecutive terms is 2/(n + 1), which tends to 0. It converges absolutely. Its value is e², using the exponential Taylor series introduced later.

title: Taylor polynomials match local behavior
goal: Build a polynomial from derivatives and attach an error guarantee.
idea: A Taylor polynomial matches a function’s value, slope, curvature and higher derivatives at a center. Close to that center, it can approximate a complicated function using arithmetic.
formula: Tₙ(x) = ∑ₖ₌₀ⁿ [f⁽ᵏ⁾(a)/k!] (x − a)ᵏ.    If |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾| ≤ M between a and x, |f(x) − Tₙ(x)| ≤ M|x − a|ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)!.
steps: For f(x) = eˣ at a = 0, every derivative at the center equals 1.
The cubic polynomial is T₃(x) = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6.
On [0, 0.2], the fourth derivative eˣ is at most e⁰·². The error bound is e⁰·²(0.2)⁴/24 ≈ 0.00008143. The actual error is about 0.00006942.
trap: Infinitely many derivatives do not automatically imply that a Taylor series equals its function. Equality requires the remainder to tend to zero. Also, degree and number of nonzero terms are different for sin and cos.
challenge: Use a cubic approximation to estimate sin(0.2), and bound the error using the degree-3 Lagrange bound.
solution: T₃(x) = x − x³/6, so T₃(0.2) = 0.198666667. Since the fourth derivative sin x has absolute value ≤ 1, the degree-3 bound gives error ≤ 0.2⁴/24 ≈ 0.000066667. A stronger bound is possible, but this one is valid.

title: A power series has a region of trust
goal: Find the radius and check both endpoints separately.
idea: A power series is an infinite polynomial centered at c. Changing x changes the numerical series. The radius describes the open interval of absolute convergence; endpoint behavior is a separate problem.
steps: The absolute ratio tends to |x − 2|, so convergence is absolute when |x − 2| < 1.
Solve: 1 < x < 3. The center is 2 and the radius is 1.
At x = 1, the series becomes ∑(−1)ⁿ/n, which converges conditionally.
At x = 3, it becomes ∑1/n, which diverges. Include 1, exclude 3: [1, 3).
trap: The ratio test cannot decide the endpoints because L = 1 there. Integrating or differentiating a power series preserves its radius, but endpoint inclusion can change.
challenge: Find the interval of convergence of ∑ₙ₌₀∞ (x + 1)ⁿ/4ⁿ.
solution: This is geometric with ratio (x + 1)/4. Require |x + 1| < 4, giving −5 < x < 3. At both endpoints the terms fail to approach zero. Radius 4, interval (−5, 3).

title: Build new series from ones you know
goal: Substitute, differentiate and integrate familiar power series within their valid intervals.
idea: You rarely need to calculate every derivative from scratch. Start with a known series and transform it, while keeping track of where the transformation is valid.
steps: Replace x by −t in the geometric series: 1/(1 + t) = 1 − t + t² − ⋯ for |t| < 1.
Integrate from 0 to x inside (−1, 1): ln(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + x³/3 − ⋯ .
At x = 0.2, the first three terms give 0.2 − 0.02 + 0.008/3 = 0.182666667.
The terms alternate and decrease. The next-term bound is 0.2⁴/4 = 0.0004. At x = 1, check separately: the alternating harmonic series converges to ln 2.
trap: A formula without its interval is incomplete. For example, the geometric series for 1/(1 − x) is not valid at x = 2 even though the rational function itself is defined there.
challenge: Find a power series for 1/(1 + x²), centered at 0, and its radius.
solution: Substitute −x² into the geometric series: ∑ₙ₌₀∞ (−1)ⁿx²ⁿ = 1 − x² + x⁴ − ⋯ for |x| < 1. Radius 1. At x = ±1 the terms fail to approach zero, so both endpoints are excluded.

idea: An infinite Taylor series is built from all derivatives at one center. It represents the function only where the Taylor remainder tends to zero.

The Taylor series is Σxⁿ/n!, converging for every real x by the ratio test.
For fixed x, the remainder is bounded by e^|x| |x|^(n+1)/(n+1)!.
This tends to zero, so the series actually equals eˣ, beyond merely converging.

title: Follow a curve using a parameter
goal: Compute tangent slopes and second derivatives when x and y both depend on t.
idea: A parameter describes how a point moves. The curve’s slope compares the rates at which y and x change: divide dy/dt by dx/dt, when dx/dt is nonzero.
formula: dy/dx = y′(t)/x′(t).    d²y/dx² = [d/dt (dy/dx)] / x′(t), when these expressions are defined.
steps: Let x = t² and y = t³, with t > 0. At t = 1 the point is (1, 1).
Differentiate: x′ = 2t and y′ = 3t². Therefore dy/dx = 3t/2.
At t = 1, the tangent line is y − 1 = (3/2)(x − 1).
Differentiate 3t/2 with respect to t, then divide by 2t: d²y/dx² = 3/(4t). At t = 1 it equals 3/4.

title: Polar curves: radius, angle and area
goal: Translate polar coordinates and use a correctly bounded polar-area integral.
idea: Polar coordinates locate a point using an angle and a signed radius. Tiny sectors have area approximately (1/2)r² dθ, which leads to a new area formula.

goal: Add vectors, find lengths and normalize a nonzero direction.
idea: A point tells you where you are. A displacement vector tells you how to move. The same vector can be drawn at many starting points without changing its components.
formula: AB = B − A.    |v| = √(v₁² + v₂² + v₃²).    Unit direction: v/|v| for v ≠ 0.
steps: Let A = (1, −2, 0) and B = (4, 2, 0). Subtract coordinates to get AB = ⟨3, 4, 0⟩.
Its length is √(9 + 16) = 5.
Divide by 5 to get the unit vector ⟨3/5, 4/5, 0⟩. Its length is 1.
Moving 10 units from A in this direction gives A + 10⟨3/5, 4/5, 0⟩ = (7, 6, 0).
trap: AB and BA have opposite signs. Normalizing the zero vector is undefined because it has no unique direction.
challenge: Find the length and unit direction of v = ⟨−2, 1, 2⟩.

questions.hint: Square each component, add, then take the square root.

questions.prompt: A unit vector always has…
questions.hint: Unit describes magnitude.
questions.explain: The length is 1; the components can be positive, negative or zero.

part: Vectors and the Geometry of Space
title: Dot products measure alignment; cross products measure area
goal: Distinguish scalar and vector products, and use projection and orientation.
idea: The dot product measures how strongly two directions align. In three dimensions, the cross product produces a vector perpendicular to both inputs, with length equal to the parallelogram’s area.
formula: u · v = |u||v|cos θ.    |u × v| = |u||v|sin θ.    projᵤv = [(v · u)/(u · u)]u, u ≠ 0.
steps: Take u = ⟨1, 2, 0⟩ and v = ⟨3, −1, 0⟩. Their dot product is 3 − 2 = 1.
Their cross product is ⟨0, 0, 1·(−1) − 2·3⟩ = ⟨0, 0, −7⟩.
The parallelogram area is 7 and the triangle area is 7/2. The negative z direction follows the right-hand rule.
The projection of v onto u is (1/5)⟨1, 2, 0⟩ = ⟨1/5, 2/5, 0⟩.
trap: u · v is a number; u × v is a vector. Swapping the cross-product order changes its sign. A zero dot product implies perpendicularity for nonzero vectors.
challenge: For u = ⟨2, 0, 0⟩ and v = ⟨0, 3, 0⟩, find the dot product and triangle area.
solution: The dot product is 0. The cross product is ⟨0, 0, 6⟩, so the triangle area is 3.

questions.hint: Multiply matching components and add.

questions.prompt: What happens to u × v if you reverse the order?
questions.hint: The cross product is anti-commutative.
questions.explain: v × u = −(u × v), with the same magnitude.

part: Vectors and the Geometry of Space
title: Lines use directions; planes use normals
goal: Write a spatial line and a plane, then find their intersection.
idea: A direction vector lies along a line. A normal vector sticks out perpendicular to a plane. Using the right vector makes the equation nearly automatic.
formula: Line: r(t) = p + tv.    Plane: n · (r − p₀) = 0, with n ≠ 0.
steps: A plane through (1, 0, 2) with normal ⟨2, −1, 3⟩ has equation 2(x − 1) − y + 3(z − 2) = 0, or 2x − y + 3z = 8.
Consider the line r(t) = ⟨0, 1, 0⟩ + t⟨1, 0, 1⟩. Its coordinates are x = t, y = 1 and z = t.
Substitute into the plane: 2t − 1 + 3t = 8, so t = 9/5.
The intersection is (9/5, 1, 9/5). Substituting it back verifies the plane equation.
trap: Do not use a plane’s normal as a direction lying in the plane. If n · v = 0, a line is parallel to the plane or lies entirely within it; check a point to distinguish those cases.
challenge: Find the plane through (0, 1, 0) with normal ⟨1, 2, −1⟩.
solution: x + 2(y − 1) − z = 0, equivalently x + 2y − z = 2.

questions.prompt: Find the distance from (1, 2, 3) to the plane z = 0.
questions.hint: This plane is the xy-plane.

questions.prompt: A line has direction v and a plane has normal n. If n · v ≠ 0, the line…
questions.hint: Substitution gives a linear equation with a nonzero t coefficient.
questions.explain: There is one parameter value satisfying the plane equation.

part: Vectors and the Geometry of Space
title: Identify surfaces through traces
goal: Identify surfaces through traces. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: A three-dimensional surface can be understood through its intersections with coordinate planes. Signs distinguish ellipsoids, hyperboloids, cones and paraboloids.
steps: Study x²+y²−z²=1.
At z=k the trace is x²+y²=1+k², a circle.
At x=0 the trace is y²−z²=1, a hyperbola.
The connected waist at z=0 identifies a one-sheet hyperboloid.
trap: A surface need not be expressible globally as z=f(x,y).
challenge: Describe z=x²+y² and its horizontal traces.
solution: It is an upward circular paraboloid; z=c gives radius √c for c≥0.

questions.prompt: For x²/4+y²/9+z²/16=1, what is the positive z-intercept?
questions.hint: Set x=y=0.
questions.explain: z²/16=1 gives z=4 on the positive axis.

questions.prompt: What are traces?
options: Intersections of a surface with chosen planes.
Only the points where all coordinates vanish.
questions.hint: A surface need not be expressible globally as z=f(x,y).
questions.explain: Intersections of a surface with chosen planes.

formulaNote: A surface need not be expressible globally as z=f(x,y).

part: Vectors and the Geometry of Space
title: Convert cylindrical and spherical coordinates
goal: Convert cylindrical and spherical coordinates. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: Cylindrical coordinates extend polar coordinates with height. In spherical coordinates, ρ is distance from the origin and φ is measured down from the positive z-axis.
formula: x=ρ sinφ cosθ; y=ρ sinφ sinθ; z=ρ cosφ
steps: The point (0,3,4) has cylindrical coordinates (r,θ,z)=(3,π/2,4).
Its spherical radius is ρ=√(9+16)=5.
The azimuth is θ=π/2 and cosφ=4/5.
Thus φ=arccos(4/5); substitute to check all coordinates.
trap: State the φ convention: some fields measure elevation from the xy-plane instead.
challenge: Convert cylindrical (2,π,−1) to Cartesian coordinates.

questions.prompt: What is the spherical radius of (2,−3,6)?
questions.hint: Use √(x²+y²+z²).

questions.prompt: In the convention used here, what is φ?
options: Angle in the xy-plane from the positive x-axis.
questions.hint: State the φ convention: some fields measure elevation from the xy-plane instead.

formulaNote: State the φ convention: some fields measure elevation from the xy-plane instead.

title: Differentiate a moving point in space
goal: Compute velocity, acceleration, speed and displacement component by component.
idea: A vector-valued function gives a position rather than a single height. Differentiate each component to get velocity; take its length to get speed.
formula: r(t) = ⟨cos t, sin t, t⟩.    v(t) = ⟨−sin t, cos t, 1⟩.    speed = |v(t)| = √2.
steps: At t = 0, the particle is at r(0) = ⟨1, 0, 0⟩.
Differentiate component by component: v(0) = ⟨0, 1, 1⟩.
Speed is √[0² + 1² + 1²] = √2. A vector and its magnitude are different objects.
Arc length from t = 0 to t = 2 is ∫₀² |v(t)| dt = 2√2. Do not integrate the velocity vector to get distance.
Differentiate velocity once more: acceleration is ⟨−cos t, −sin t, 0⟩. Constant speed does not mean zero acceleration; the direction changes.
trap: Speed is not the derivative of |r(t)|. The derivative of the distance from the origin only measures motion toward or away from the origin.
challenge: For r(t) = ⟨3t, 4t, 0⟩, find speed and distance traveled on 0 ≤ t ≤ 2.
solution: v(t) = ⟨3, 4, 0⟩, so speed is 5 and distance is ∫₀²5 dt = 10.

questions.prompt: For r(t) = ⟨t, t², 0⟩, what is speed at t = 0?
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then take the length.

questions.prompt: What is the geometric direction of r′(t), when nonzero?
questions.hint: Velocity points along instantaneous motion.
questions.explain: The derivative is a tangent vector in the direction of increasing t.

title: Integrate a vector-valued function componentwise
goal: Integrate a vector-valued function componentwise. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: Vector integration accumulates each coordinate, with a vector constant determined by initial conditions. Definite velocity integrals give displacement rather than distance.
steps: Given r′(t)=⟨2t,3,t²⟩ and r(0)=⟨1,0,−1⟩, integrate each coordinate.
Obtain r(t)=⟨t²+C₁,3t+C₂,t³/3+C₃⟩.
Initial data give C₁=1,C₂=0,C₃=−1.
Differentiate the resulting vector to verify it.
trap: The magnitude of a velocity integral generally differs from the integral of speed.
challenge: Find displacement from t=0 to 2 if v=⟨1,t,0⟩.
solution: Integrate components to get ⟨2,2,0⟩.

questions.prompt: For v=⟨2t,1,0⟩ on [0,2], what is the x-displacement?
questions.hint: Integrate the first component.

questions.prompt: How many constants appear in a general three-component antiderivative?
options: Three scalar constants, forming one vector constant.
Only one identical scalar added to every component.
questions.hint: The magnitude of a velocity integral generally differs from the integral of speed.
questions.explain: Three scalar constants, forming one vector constant.

formulaNote: The magnitude of a velocity integral generally differs from the integral of speed.

title: Separate tangential and normal motion
goal: Separate tangential and normal motion. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: The unit tangent points along velocity. Its change determines the principal normal where T′≠0; acceleration can have tangential and normal components.
steps: For r(t)=⟨2cos t,2sin t,0⟩, speed is 2.
T=⟨−sin t,cos t,0⟩.
T′=⟨−cos t,−sin t,0⟩ already has unit length, so it equals N.
Acceleration is 2N: no tangential acceleration and normal magnitude 2.
trap: The principal normal is undefined where T′=0; a straight segment has no uniquely determined principal normal.
challenge: Find T and N at t=0 for the same circle.

questions.prompt: For speed v=3 on a circle of radius 3, what is the normal acceleration?
questions.hint: Use aₙ=v²/R.

questions.prompt: What is the tangential acceleration component?
questions.hint: The principal normal is undefined where T′=0; a straight segment has no uniquely determined principal normal.

formulaNote: The principal normal is undefined where T′=0; a straight segment has no uniquely determined principal normal.

title: Distance and bending along a curve
goal: Compute arc length and distinguish curvature from speed.
idea: A curve can be traveled quickly or slowly without changing its shape. Speed measures the parameterization’s pace. Curvature measures how rapidly the unit tangent changes per unit distance.
formula: L = ∫ₐᵇ |r′(t)| dt.    κ = |r′ × r″| / |r′|³ for a regular twice-differentiable spatial curve.
steps: For r(t) = ⟨3cos t, 3sin t, 0⟩, the velocity is ⟨−3sin t, 3cos t, 0⟩ and its length is 3.
On 0 ≤ t ≤ π, arc length is ∫₀π3 dt = 3π: half a circle of radius 3.
Acceleration is ⟨−3cos t, −3sin t, 0⟩. The cross-product magnitude |r′ × r″| is 9.
Curvature is 9/27 = 1/3. Reparameterizing the circle changes speed but not its curvature at a point.
trap: The integral of r′ gives displacement, a vector. The integral of |r′| gives distance. Curvature formulas with |r′| in the denominator require nonzero velocity.
challenge: Find the curvature of a circle of radius 5.
solution: For any circle of radius R, curvature is 1/R. Here it is 1/5.

questions.prompt: A particle travels a circle of radius 2 once. Enter its distance divided by π.
questions.hint: Use the circumference, 2πR.
questions.explain: Distance is 4π, even though net displacement is zero.

questions.prompt: A particle moves around a circle at constant nonzero speed. Its acceleration…
options: Is always tangent to the circle.
Has no relation to the path.
questions.hint: The velocity’s direction is still changing.
questions.explain: For uniform circular motion the acceleration is centripetal, perpendicular to velocity.

title: Read a surface through its level curves
goal: Recognize domains and interpret contour curves as constant heights.
idea: A function of two variables assigns a height to each point in its domain. Contours are slices at fixed heights; they compress a three-dimensional surface into a readable map.
formula: A level curve of f is the set f(x, y) = c.    For f(x, y) = x² + 4y², contours are ellipses.
steps: For z = x² + 4y², every (x, y) is allowed, so the domain is all of ℝ².
The height at (1, 1) is 5.
At height c = 4, the contour is x² + 4y² = 4, or x²/4 + y² = 1.
At y = 0, the vertical slice is z = x². At x = 0, it is z = 4y², which rises faster as |y| grows.
trap: A contour is not a particle’s path unless you explicitly choose to move along it. Contour spacing indicates steepness only when the contour height increments are comparable.
challenge: Find the domain of f(x, y) = √(9 − x² − y²).
solution: Require 9 − x² − y² ≥ 0. The domain is the closed disk x² + y² ≤ 9, including its boundary.

questions.prompt: For f(x, y) = x² + 4y², find f(2, 1).
questions.hint: Substitute both coordinates.

questions.prompt: For f(x, y) = ln(y − x²), the domain requires…
questions.hint: The logarithm’s argument must be strictly positive.
questions.explain: y − x² > 0, so the boundary parabola is excluded.

title: A limit must survive every approach path
goal: Use disagreeing paths to disprove a limit, and a bound to prove one.
idea: Near a point in the plane, there are infinitely many ways to approach. Two paths giving different limits disprove a common limit. Two paths agreeing do not prove one.
formula: If two approach paths give different limiting values, the multivariable limit does not exist.
steps: For f(x, y) = xy/(x² + y²) away from (0, 0), approach on y = 0. The value is 0.
Approach on y = x. The value is 1/2 for x ≠ 0. The limits disagree, so there is no limit at the origin.
For g(x, y) = x²y/(x² + y²), use a bound instead: |g(x, y)| ≤ |y|.
Since |y| ≤ √(x² + y²) → 0, the squeeze theorem proves g → 0 along every path.
trap: Checking only the x- and y-axes can miss a diagonal or curved path. A successful proof needs control over every nearby point, not a large collection of examples.
challenge: Does h(x, y) = x²y/(x⁴ + y²) have a limit at the origin?
solution: No. On y = 0 it is 0, while on y = x² it is 1/2 for x ≠ 0. Both paths approach the origin.

questions.prompt: For xy/(x² + y²), what value occurs on y = −x, x ≠ 0?
questions.hint: Substitute y = −x and cancel x².

questions.prompt: The limit agrees on both coordinate axes. What follows?
questions.hint: A diagonal path may behave differently.
questions.explain: Agreement on two paths is necessary for a common limit but not sufficient.

title: One surface, many partial derivatives
goal: Calculate first and mixed partials, interpret slices and distinguish partial from total change.
idea: A surface z = f(x, y) has no single slope. Choose a direction first. For fₓ, freeze y and vary x; for fᵧ, freeze x and vary y.
formula: f(x, y) = x² + xy + y².    fₓ = 2x + y.    fᵧ = x + 2y.    ∇f = ⟨fₓ, fᵧ⟩.
steps: At (1, 2), the height is f(1, 2) = 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.
Along the x direction, freeze y = 2: the slice is z = x² + 2x + 4. Its slope at x = 1 is 4.
Along the y direction, freeze x = 1: z = 1 + y + y². Its slope at y = 2 is 5.
For this polynomial, fₓₓ = 2, fᵧᵧ = 2 and fₓᵧ = fᵧₓ = 1. Equality of mixed partials is guaranteed when the relevant mixed partials are continuous in a neighborhood.
trap: Treat the other variable as a constant, not as zero. For ∂(xy)/∂x the result is y. A directional derivative uses a unit direction vector.
challenge: For f(x, y) = x²y + sin y, find fₓ(2, 0) and fᵧ(2, 0).
solution: fₓ = 2xy, so fₓ(2, 0) = 0. fᵧ = x² + cos y, so fᵧ(2, 0) = 5.

questions.prompt: For f(x, y) = x²y, what is fₓ(2, 3)?
questions.hint: Differentiate in x while holding y fixed.

questions.prompt: For a differentiable f and unit vector u, Dᵤf equals…
questions.hint: Project the gradient onto the chosen unit direction.
questions.explain: The dot product ∇f · u gives the rate of change along that direction. Its maximum is |∇f|.

title: A tangent plane is a local prediction machine
goal: Use linearization to estimate nearby function values and interpret differentials.
idea: A differentiable surface looks nearly planar when you zoom in. Its two partial derivatives tell you how changes in x and y combine to produce a first-order change in height.
formula: L(x, y) = f(a, b) + fₓ(a, b)(x − a) + fᵧ(a, b)(y − b).    df = fₓ dx + fᵧ dy.
steps: Let f(x, y) = √(x² + y²). At (3, 4), the height is 5.
The partials are fₓ = x/√(x² + y²) and fᵧ = y/√(x² + y²), giving 3/5 and 4/5.
Predict f(3.02, 3.99) ≈ 5.004. This is a local approximation, not an exact identity.
trap: Existing partial derivatives alone do not guarantee differentiability. Continuous partials in a neighborhood are a useful sufficient condition. A tangent-plane estimate needs a differentiable function at the center.
challenge: Linearize f(x, y) = x² + y² at (1, 2) and estimate f(1.01, 1.98).
solution: L = 5 + 2(x − 1) + 4(y − 2). The estimate is 5 + 0.02 − 0.08 = 4.94. The exact value is 4.9405, so the error here is 0.0005.

questions.prompt: For f = x² + y² at (1, 2), dx = 0.1 and dy = 0, what is df?
questions.hint: Use fₓ(1, 2) = 2 and fᵧ(1, 2) = 4.
questions.explain: df = 2(0.1) + 4(0) = 0.2. The exact height change would be 0.21.

questions.prompt: A linearization is generally most reliable…
options: Near its center, where differentiability holds.
questions.hint: It captures first-order local behavior.
questions.explain: Moving farther away can make the neglected higher-order terms significant.

title: The chain rule adds every route of change
goal: Differentiate a multivariable quantity when its inputs change together.
idea: If z depends on x and y, and both depend on time, then time affects z along two routes. Add the contribution from each route.
formula: For differentiable f and paths: dz/dt = fₓ dx/dt + fᵧ dy/dt, evaluated along (x(t), y(t)).
steps: Let z = x²y, with x = t and y = t².
The partials are fₓ = 2xy and fᵧ = x². The path derivatives are dx/dt = 1 and dy/dt = 2t.
Substitute the path: dz/dt = (2t·t²)(1) + (t²)(2t) = 4t³.
Check directly: z(t) = t²·t² = t⁴, whose derivative is 4t³. At t = 2 the rate is 32.
trap: A partial derivative holds other independent variables fixed. A total derivative follows their actual changes. Do not take fₓ alone when y is also changing.
challenge: For z = xy, x = eᵗ and y = t², find dz/dt at t = 0.
solution: dz/dt = y eᵗ + x(2t) = eᵗ(t² + 2t). At t = 0 it is 0.

questions.prompt: If z = x² + y², x = t and y = 2t, find dz/dt at t = 1.
questions.hint: Direct substitution gives z = 5t².
questions.explain: dz/dt = 10t, so the value at 1 is 10.

questions.prompt: In z = f(x(t), y(t)), the partials fₓ and fᵧ are evaluated…
options: At (t, t), regardless of the path.
questions.hint: The path tells you where on the surface you are.
questions.explain: Evaluate the partial derivatives at the current path coordinates before combining the rates.

title: The gradient turns direction into a rate
goal: Normalize a direction and calculate directional derivatives and steepest ascent.
idea: The gradient bundles all partial derivatives into one vector. Dot it with a unit direction to obtain the rate of change per unit distance in that direction.
formula: Dᵤf = ∇f · u for |u| = 1 and differentiable f.    Maximum directional derivative = |∇f|.
steps: For f(x, y) = x² + 2y², the gradient at (1, 1) is ⟨2, 4⟩.
To move in direction v = ⟨3, 4⟩, first normalize: u = ⟨3/5, 4/5⟩.
The directional derivative is 2(3/5) + 4(4/5) = 22/5 = 4.4.
Steepest ascent is along ⟨1/√5, 2/√5⟩, with rate √20 = 2√5. A vector tangent to a smooth level curve is perpendicular to the nonzero gradient.
trap: Using a nonunit vector changes the rate by its length. At a critical point where ∇f = 0, all first-order directional derivatives vanish; this alone does not classify the point.
challenge: For f(x, y) = 3x − 4y, find the maximum directional derivative and its direction.
solution: The gradient is ⟨3, −4⟩ with length 5. The maximum rate is 5, in unit direction ⟨3/5, −4/5⟩.

questions.prompt: At (1, 1) for f = x² + 2y², what is the rate in unit direction ⟨1, 0⟩?
questions.hint: Take the dot product with ⟨2, 4⟩.

questions.prompt: For a nonzero gradient, moving perpendicular to it gives…
questions.hint: Perpendicular vectors have dot product zero.
questions.explain: The instantaneous first-order rate is zero; the function can still change at higher order.

title: Use a gradient as a surface normal
goal: Use a gradient as a surface normal. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: At a regular point of F(x,y,z)=c, the gradient is perpendicular to the tangent plane. It also supplies the direction of the normal line.
steps: For the sphere F=x²+y²+z²=9 at p=(1,2,2), ∇F(p)=⟨2,4,4⟩.
The tangent plane is 2(x−1)+4(y−2)+4(z−2)=0.
Simplify to x+2y+2z=9.
A normal line is r=(1,2,2)+t⟨1,2,2⟩, using a proportional direction.
trap: A zero gradient does not determine a unique tangent plane by this formula.
challenge: Find the tangent plane to x²+y²+z²=4 at (0,0,2).
solution: The gradient is ⟨0,0,4⟩, giving z=2.

questions.prompt: At (1,2,2), what is |∇(x²+y²+z²)|?
questions.hint: The gradient is twice the radius vector.

questions.prompt: What hypothesis is needed for the regular-level-surface formula?
options: The gradient at the point is nonzero.
Every partial derivative at the point is zero.
questions.hint: A zero gradient does not determine a unique tangent plane by this formula.
questions.explain: The gradient at the point is nonzero.

formulaNote: A zero gradient does not determine a unique tangent plane by this formula.

title: Classify critical points without guessing from a picture
goal: Use the second-derivative test and include boundaries in global-extremum problems.
idea: Zero gradient identifies candidates, not automatic maxima or minima. Second derivatives describe the local bending. For absolute extrema on a closed bounded region, also inspect its boundary.
formula: D = fₓₓfᵧᵧ − (fₓᵧ)² at a critical point.    D > 0: min if fₓₓ > 0, max if fₓₓ < 0.    D < 0: saddle.    D = 0: inconclusive.
steps: For f(x, y) = x² + xy + y² − 4x − 2y, solve fₓ = 2x + y − 4 = 0 and fᵧ = x + 2y − 2 = 0.
The only critical point is (2, 0), with f(2, 0) = −4.
Second derivatives give fₓₓ = 2, fᵧᵧ = 2 and fₓᵧ = 1. Thus D = 4 − 1 = 3 > 0 and fₓₓ > 0: a local minimum.
In fact, with u = x − 2, f = (u + y/2)² + 3y²/4 − 4. The squared terms are nonnegative and vanish together only at (2, 0), proving this is the global minimum.
trap: D = 0 is not a conclusion. For example x⁴ + y⁴ has a minimum at the origin while x⁴ − y⁴ has a saddle there; both give D = 0.
challenge: Classify the critical point of f(x, y) = x² − y² at the origin.
solution: fₓₓ = 2, fᵧᵧ = −2 and fₓᵧ = 0, so D = −4 < 0. The origin is a saddle: values rise along the x-axis and fall along the y-axis.

questions.prompt: At a critical point, fₓₓ = 4, fᵧᵧ = 3 and fₓᵧ = 2. Find D.
questions.hint: Subtract the square of the mixed partial from the product of the pure partials.
questions.explain: D = 4·3 − 2² = 8. Since fₓₓ > 0, it is a local minimum under the test’s smoothness assumptions.

questions.prompt: To find absolute extrema of a continuous function on a closed disk, inspect…
options: Only the point with the largest x-coordinate.
questions.hint: The best value may lie on the edge.
questions.explain: An absolute extremum can occur in the interior or on the boundary.

title: Optimize with feasible regions and boundaries
goal: Optimize with feasible regions and boundaries. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: An application needs an objective, a feasible set, interior candidates, and boundary analysis. Different boundaries can require different one-variable parameterizations.
formula: Absolute extrema: compare interior and boundary candidates
steps: Maximize f(x,y)=xy where x,y≥0 and x+y≤6.
The interior equations y=0,x=0 give no candidate in the strict interior.
On x=0 or y=0, f=0.
On x+y=6, f=x(6−x), whose maximum is 9 at (3,3).
trap: A compact feasible set and continuity guarantee extrema, but not that they occur at an interior critical point.
challenge: Maximize xy on x,y≥0 with x+y≤8.
solution: On the slanted edge, x(8−x) is maximized at x=4,y=4, giving 16; the other edges give zero.

questions.prompt: What is max xy on x,y≥0, x+y≤10?
questions.hint: Analyze x+y=10 and the other edges.
questions.explain: x(10−x) reaches 25 at (5,5); axis edges give 0.

questions.prompt: Must a global maximum have zero gradient?
options: Yes, even on the edge of the feasible set.
No; it may lie on a boundary.
questions.hint: A compact feasible set and continuity guarantee extrema, but not that they occur at an interior critical point.
questions.explain: No; it may lie on a boundary.

formulaNote: A compact feasible set and continuity guarantee extrema, but not that they occur at an interior critical point.

title: Optimize while staying on a constraint
goal: Use Lagrange multipliers and compare all candidates on a regular constraint.
idea: At a constrained extremum on a smooth curve with nonzero constraint gradient, there is no improvement along the curve’s tangent. The objective gradient must therefore align with the constraint’s normal.
formula: For g(x, y) = c with ∇g ≠ 0, solve ∇f = λ∇g together with g = c. Then compare candidate values.
steps: Maximize and minimize f(x, y) = xy on x² + y² = 1. The equations are y = 2λx and x = 2λy, plus the circle constraint.
Neither x nor y can be zero in a solution of these gradient equations on the circle. Combining them gives λ = ±1/2.
For λ = 1/2, y = x, giving (±1/√2, ±1/√2) with matching signs and f = 1/2.
For λ = −1/2, y = −x, giving opposite signs and f = −1/2. The circle is compact, so these largest and smallest candidate values are the global extrema.
trap: Do not silently divide by x or y and lose zero-coordinate candidates in other problems. Singular constraint points, boundaries and inequality constraints need separate attention.
challenge: Maximize x + y on x² + y² = 2.
solution: The equations 1 = 2λx and 1 = 2λy imply x = y. The candidates are (1, 1) and (−1, −1). Compare values: maximum 2 at (1, 1), minimum −2 at (−1, −1).

questions.prompt: What is the maximum of xy on x² + y² = 1?
questions.hint: Try x = y, then apply the circle constraint.
questions.explain: At equal-sign coordinates of magnitude 1/√2, the product is 1/2.

questions.hint: The point must still be feasible.
questions.explain: Gradient alignment does not by itself ensure that the candidate lies on the constraint.

title: Describe a plane region with iterated bounds
goal: Describe a plane region with iterated bounds. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: An iterated integral adds slices. Inner bounds may depend on the outer variable; reversing order requires describing the same region again.
steps: Let D satisfy 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤x.
Its area is ∫₀¹∫₀ˣ1 dy dx=∫₀¹x dx=1/2.
To reverse order, use 0≤y≤1 and y≤x≤1.
Then ∫₀¹∫ᵧ¹1 dx dy=∫₀¹(1−y)dy=1/2.
trap: Reversing dy dx does not merely swap the old bounds.
challenge: Write both orders for 0≤y≤2 and 0≤x≤y.
solution: ∫₀²∫₀ʸ1 dx dy and ∫₀²∫ₓ²1 dy dx both give 2.

questions.hint: Integrate the slice height x.

title: Integrate height over a plane region

idea: A double integral accumulates density or signed height over area. For continuous functions on suitable bounded regions, iterated integrals compute it.

First ∫₀²(x+y)dy=2x+2.
Then ∫₀¹(2x+2)dx=3.
Because f≥0 here, the result is the volume under its graph.

solution: ∫₀²x dx·∫₀¹y dy=2·(1/2)=1.

title: Include the polar area factor

title: Compute lamina mass, moments and inertia
goal: Compute lamina mass, moments and inertia. Explain your method and its conditions.

Divide by mass to get x̄=5/9.
Symmetry in y gives ȳ=1/2.

solution: ∫₀¹∫₀¹y² dy dx=1/3.

title: Measure the area of a graph surface
goal: Measure the area of a graph surface. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: A sloping graph stretches a small base rectangle. The stretching factor depends on both partial derivatives.
steps: For z=2x+y over the unit square, fₓ=2 and fᵧ=1.
The area multiplier is √(1+4+1)=√6.
Integrating this constant over base area 1 gives surface area √6.
This exceeds the base area, as a tilted plane should.

solution: Both partials vanish, so the factor is 1 and the area is 8.

questions.hint: The surface area is √(1+1+0).

title: Accumulate volume and density in space
goal: Accumulate volume and density in space. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: Triple integrals add contributions from small volume cells. Bounds describe the solid, and integrating 1 gives its volume.
steps: Let E be 0≤x≤1,0≤y≤2,0≤z≤3 with density ρ=z.
Integrating first in z gives ∫₀³z dz=9/2.
The remaining xy-base area is 2.
The mass is 9; the solid’s volume is 6.

solution: Use 0≤x≤1,0≤y≤1−x,0≤z≤1−x−y. Integrating gives 1/6.

title: Use cylindrical and spherical volume elements

formula: dV=r dr dθ dz; dV=ρ²sinφ dρ dφ dθ
steps: For a radius-2 ball, use 0≤ρ≤2,0≤φ≤π,0≤θ≤2π.
Volume is ∫₀²π∫₀^π∫₀²ρ²sinφ dρ dφ dθ.
The factors are 2π,2,8/3.
Their product is 32π/3, the familiar ball volume.

title: Transform regions and track local area scaling
goal: Transform regions and track local area scaling. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: A change of variables reshapes both the region and integrand. The absolute determinant measures local area scaling; a one-to-one regular transformation avoids unintended multiplicity.
steps: Set x=u+v,y=u−v for 0≤u≤1,0≤v≤1.
The Jacobian determinant is (1)(−1)−(1)(1)=−2.
Its absolute value is 2.
The image parallelogram therefore has area ∫₀¹∫₀¹2 du dv=2.
trap: Use the Jacobian in the direction x,y as functions of u,v; reversing the direction gives its reciprocal where defined.
challenge: For x=2u,y=3v, find the area of the image of the unit square.
solution: The determinant is 6, so the image area is 6.

title: Read a vector field and its derivatives
goal: Read a vector field and its derivatives. Explain your method and its conditions.

steps: For F=⟨−y,x,0⟩, arrows turn around the z-axis.
Divergence is 0+0+0=0.

title: Distinguish scalar line integrals from work
goal: Distinguish scalar line integrals from work. Explain your method and its conditions.

steps: For F=⟨y,x⟩ and r(t)=⟨t,t²⟩ on [0,1], substitute F(r)=⟨t²,t⟩.
The velocity is ⟨1,2t⟩.
Their dot product is 3t².
Work is ∫₀¹3t² dt=1; reversing the path gives −1.

title: Use a potential to evaluate path-independent work
goal: Use a potential to evaluate path-independent work. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: A gradient field has work equal to the potential change. On a simply connected open domain, a continuously differentiable curl-free field is conservative; domain holes can invalidate the converse.
steps: For F=⟨2xy,x²⟩, integrate the first component in x to get φ=x²y+g(y).
Match φᵧ=x²+g′(y) to x², so g is constant.
Any piecewise smooth path with these endpoints gives the same work.

challenge: For φ=x²+y², find work of ∇φ from (0,0) to (1,2).

title: Replace planar circulation by an area integral
goal: Replace planar circulation by an area integral. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: Green’s theorem relates circulation around a positively oriented boundary to a scalar curl over its interior. Smoothness must hold throughout the region, and holes have oppositely oriented inner boundaries.
steps: For P=−y/2 and Q=x/2, Qₓ−Pᵧ=1.
On the counterclockwise unit circle, Green’s theorem gives ∮P dx+Q dy=∬disk1 dA.
The result is π.
Direct parameterization x=cos t,y=sin t gives integrand 1/2, whose full-period integral is also π.

challenge: Find circulation of F=⟨−y,x⟩ around a counterclockwise radius-2 circle.
solution: The scalar curl is 2, so circulation is 2·4π=8π.

title: Describe a surface using two parameters
goal: Describe a surface using two parameters. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: Two independent parameters trace a surface patch. Their partial derivative vectors span the tangent plane; a nonzero cross product supplies both a normal direction and area scaling.
steps: For r(u,v)=⟨u,v,u+v⟩ on the unit square, rᵤ=⟨1,0,1⟩ and rᵥ=⟨0,1,1⟩.
Their cross product is ⟨−1,−1,1⟩.
Its magnitude is √3, so the patch area is √3.
Reversing the parameter order flips the normal but preserves this magnitude.

challenge: Parameterize the cylinder x²+y²=4, 0≤z≤3.
solution: r(θ,z)=⟨2cosθ,2sinθ,z⟩ with 0≤θ≤2π,0≤z≤3; identify the seam rather than counting another full turn.

title: Convert outward flux to a volume integral
goal: Convert outward flux to a volume integral. Explain your method and its conditions.

Its divergence is 3.
Outward flux is 3 times ball volume 4π/3, giving 4π.
Directly on the sphere, F equals the outward unit normal, so flux also equals sphere area 4π.

Its induced boundary runs counterclockwise as seen from above.

title: Recover a potential for an exact differential equation

Integrate M in x: ψ=x²+xy+g(y).
Match ψᵧ=x+g′(y) to x+2y, giving g=y².
Solutions lie on x²+xy+y²=C; an initial point determines the constant.

title: Solve constant-coefficient homogeneous equations
goal: Solve constant-coefficient homogeneous equations. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: For ay″+by′+cy=0, exponential trials lead to a characteristic polynomial. Distinct, repeated and complex roots produce different independent solution pairs.

The characteristic equation (r−1)(r−2)=0 gives r=1,2.
Thus y=C₁eˣ+C₂e^(2x).

The homogeneous solution is C₁eˣ+C₂e⁻ˣ.

title: Solve a differential equation with a coefficient recurrence
goal: Solve a differential equation with a coefficient recurrence. Explain your method and its conditions.
idea: At an ordinary point, a power-series ansatz converts a differential equation into coefficient relations. Shift indices carefully and discuss convergence rather than treating formal algebra alone as a full solution.
steps: For y′=y and y(0)=2, insert the two series.
Matching xⁿ coefficients gives (n+1)aₙ₊₁=aₙ.
Starting from a₀=2 gives a₁=2,a₂=1,a₃=1/3 and generally aₙ=2/n!.
Thus y=2Σxⁿ/n!=2eˣ, whose convergence for all x follows from the ratio test.
